headline: High-risk shared-state and broad-egress pair can leak or corrupt work products; prompt-injection risk is lower but present via file-based handoff.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Dify can read/write filesystem and ingest uploaded knowledge-base files, while firecrawl exposes scraped web content and MCP-compatible client support. If Dify consumes firecrawl output through files or shared datastore, attacker-controlled page content can become instructions. The interaction is inferred from documented surfaces, not directly reproduced.
conditions: IF firecrawl output is written into a file or datastore that Dify later treats as instructions
IF Dify workflows parse scraped HTML/markdown without provenance filtering
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to all firecrawl outputs before Dify ingests them
Restrict Dify prompts to ignore instructions inside retrieved content
Use a separate staging folder for scraped content
Manually review one sample scrape before enabling automation

B_data_leakage.rationale: Dify touches knowledge-base content, conversation logs, and model-provider/tool secrets; firecrawl touches web content, screenshots, structured data, and API keys. A shared workspace or copied artifacts could move sensitive material between them, and both have broad network egress. The pairwise leakage path is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF Dify exports conversation logs or KB files into a location firecrawl can read
IF firecrawl stores scraped pages or screenshots in a shared workspace accessible to Dify
mitigations: Separate storage buckets for Dify and firecrawl artifacts
Rotate any API keys that may appear in scraped pages
Disable automatic ingestion of raw scrape outputs into Dify
Review one end-to-end transfer path for secrets before rollout

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Dify has filesystem write and subprocess execution; firecrawl is an API client/CLI with MCP-compatible support and broad egress. If both are pointed at the same mutable workspace, they can overwrite each other's artifacts or race on shared files. No locking is documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or git checkout
IF an orchestrator launches them concurrently without file locks
mitigations: Assign distinct working directories
Add a simple lock file around shared outputs
Disable concurrent writes during initial testing
Check for clobbered files after one trial run

D_cascading_error.rationale: Dify can generate agent/workflow outputs that firecrawl may consume through its API/CLI flow, and firecrawl can then act on those outputs as scrape/search parameters. Without an explicit verification step, malformed or hallucinated instructions can cascade from Dify into firecrawl actions. The pairwise handoff is inferred from documented tool-use patterns.
conditions: IF firecrawl is configured to execute URLs, queries, or crawl targets produced by Dify
IF no validation step checks Dify output before firecrawl uses it
mitigations: Insert a schema validator between Dify and firecrawl
Require human approval for the first few automated runs
Limit firecrawl to an allowlist of domains
Log rejected Dify outputs for review

E_compliance.rationale: Dify explicitly handles conversation logs, knowledge-base content, and model-provider/tool secrets; firecrawl handles web content, screenshots, structured data, and API keys. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a low compliance concern is visible from documented retention-sensitive data handling. The other agent is cited because the risk is pairwise data flow, not a single-agent issue.
conditions: IF regulated data is scraped by firecrawl and then stored in Dify logs or KB files
IF retention settings differ between the two systems for the same data class
mitigations: Classify data before sending it to either agent
Set a short retention window for logs and scrape artifacts
Document which system is the system of record
Review one sample record for residency and retention fields
